On one occasion, however, the lieutenant asked why he had travelled so far across the ice in such an unusual vehicle.

His face immediately took on an expression of profound despair, and he answered, “To find someone who ran away from me.”

“And was the man you were pursuing travelling in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I believe we have seen him. The day before we rescued you, we saw dogs pulling a sledge across the ice, with a man riding in it.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked question after question about the route taken by the demon, as he called him. Shortly afterward, when we were alone together, he said, “I have undoubtedly awakened your curiosity, as well as that of these kind people, but you are too considerate to question me.”

“Certainly. It would be both intrusive and cruel of me to trouble you simply to satisfy my own curiosity.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous predicament. Through your kindness, you have brought me back to life.”

A little later he asked whether I thought the breakup of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I told him I could not answer with any certainty, since the ice had not broken until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety before then. But I had no way of knowing whether he had.

From that moment, a new spark of life seemed to animate the stranger’s failing body. He showed the greatest eagerness to go on deck and look out for the sledge we had previously seen. I have persuaded him to stay in the cabin, however, because he is much too weak to withstand the bitter air. I have promised to have someone keep watch on his behalf and tell him immediately if anything new comes into view.

This is my account of everything connected with this strange event up to the present day. The stranger’s health has gradually improved, but he says very little and seems troubled whenever anyone other than me enters his cabin. Yet his manner is so gentle and accommodating that all the sailors take an interest in him, although they have scarcely spoken with him. For my part, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant, profound sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in happier days, since even in his present shattered condition he remains so appealing and kind.

I told you in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the wide ocean. Yet I have found a man whom, before misery broke his spirit, I would gladly have welcomed as a brother of my heart.

Mr. Otis was considerably upset by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the kindly nobleman remained firm. Eventually he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her. And when, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first court reception following her marriage, everyone admired her jewels. For Virginia acquired the coronet that is the reward of all good little American girls, and married her young sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming and so deeply in love that everyone was delighted with the marriage, except the elderly Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had hosted no fewer than three expensive dinner parties for that purpose—and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis was extremely fond of the young Duke personally, but he objected to titles in principle. In his own words, he ‘had some fear that the weakening influence of an aristocracy devoted to pleasure might cause the true principles of republican simplicity to be forgotten.’ His objections were completely overruled, however, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, his daughter leaning on his arm, no man anywhere in England could have been prouder.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went to Canterville Chase. The afternoon after they arrived, they walked to the secluded churchyard beside the pine woods. At first there had been considerable difficulty deciding what to put on Sir Simon’s gravestone. Eventually it had been agreed to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some beautiful roses, which she scattered over the grave. After standing beside it for a while, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. There the Duchess sat on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up into her lovely eyes. Suddenly he tossed his cigarette aside, took her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife ought to have no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.’

‘Yes, you do,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never told me what happened when you were locked away with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ Virginia said seriously.

One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, a note arrived in the post. The very sight of its envelope sent me into a flutter: although I had never seen the handwriting of the address before, I instinctively knew whose it was. It had no conventional opening—Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything—but read as follows:

“I am coming to London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you would meet me? At any rate, Miss Havisham thinks so, and I am writing in accordance with her wishes. She sends her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Had there been time, I would probably have ordered several new suits for the occasion. As there was not, I had to make do with the clothes I already owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I had neither peace nor rest until the day came. Its arrival brought me neither, either: I was worse than ever, and began lurking around the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew this perfectly well, I still felt it was dangerous to let the office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a stretch. In this irrational state I had completed the first half hour of a watch lasting four or five hours when Wemmick came upon me.

“Hello, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I would hardly have expected this to be your usual territory.”

I explained that I was waiting for someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both thriving, thank you,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He’s in wonderful spirits. Eighty-two on his next birthday. I’m thinking of firing eighty-two shots, provided the neighbours don’t complain and my cannon can withstand the pressure. Still, that’s no subject for London conversation. Where do you suppose I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, since he was heading that way.

“The next best thing,” Wemmick answered. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re handling a case about a banker’s parcel just now. I’ve been down the road to take a look at the scene, and now I must have a few words with our client.”

“Did your client carry out the robbery?” I asked.

“Good heavens, no,” Wemmick replied very dryly. “But he is accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us could be accused of it, you know.”
